standard_prerequisites.name: Term and its value under an assignment
standard_prerequisites.statement: Terms are built from constants, variables and function symbols; the value of a term in a structure M under an assignment s is defined by the obvious recursion on the term.
standard_prerequisites.use: The induction follows the term construction and the value function is unfolded twice in the composite case (source lines 926-955).

standard_prerequisites.name: Substitution of a term for a variable
standard_prerequisites.statement: The result of substituting the term t' for the variable x throughout the term t, defined by recursion on t, leaving constants in place and replacing exactly the variable x.
standard_prerequisites.use: The substitution is computed in each of the four cases (source lines 929, 933, 938, 946).

standard_prerequisites.name: Modified variable assignment
standard_prerequisites.statement: The assignment that agrees with s everywhere except at x, where it takes a prescribed value.
standard_prerequisites.use: The right-hand side of the identity uses the modified assignment at every case, and the variable cases are decided by which variables the two assignments agree on (source lines 934-940).

core_obligations: Constant case: if t is a constant c, then the substituted term is still c, and both sides evaluate to the interpretation of c independently of the assignment (source lines 929-931).

Variable case other than x: if t is a variable y different from x, the substituted term is y, and both sides take the value of y because the modified assignment agrees with s at y (source lines 933-936).
The substituted variable itself: if t is x, the substituted term is t', and the right-hand side is exactly the value of t' under s by the definition of the modified assignment (source lines 938-940).

Composite case: if t is f applied to t_1, ..., t_n, unfold the value of the substituted composite term into the interpretation of f applied to the values of the substituted subterms, apply the induction hypothesis to each subterm, and fold the result back into the value of the original composite under the modified assignment (source lines 942-957).

proof_roadmap.step: Constant case: substitution does nothing and both sides are the interpretation of the constant.
Variable case y different from x: both assignments agree at y.
Case t = x: the substituted term is t' and the modified assignment has exactly that value at x.
Composite case: two definitional unfoldings around the induction hypothesis applied to all immediate subterms.

difficulty_reason: The counted unit is the author's own proposition prop:ext-terms at source lines 920-924: the semantic value of the term obtained by substituting t' for x in t, evaluated under an assignment s, equals the value of t evaluated under the assignment that differs from s only at x, where it takes the value of t'. The proof at source lines 926-959 is a structural induction on the term t and it is the substitution lemma of first-order semantics, so it is a real bookkeeping argument rather than a one-step unfolding. The four cases are not symmetric: the constant case is immediate, the variable case other than x needs the observation that the modified assignment agrees with s at that variable, the case t = x needs the definition of the modified assignment at the substituted variable itself, and the composite case needs the induction hypothesis applied simultaneously to all the immediate subterms together with two definitional unfoldings of the value function, arranged with explicit annotations in a displayed chain of equalities. Nothing in the statement indicates which case needs which observation. No result outside the retained text is used.

compared.difference: prop:valindep (in the same unit) counts the independence of a term's value from the parts of the assignment that are not free in the term; our candidate is the substitution lemma, relating two different assignments through a substitution, and the proof does not reduce to the independence statement.
prop:entails-unsat is a semantic relation between entailment and unsatisfiability; our candidate is a syntactic-semantic commutation property of substitution and term evaluation.
